arguments.summary: Policy exposure is more direct for NVDA: its August 2026 filing says it was effectively foreclosed from China data-center compute despite the January case-by-case licensing rule. MU discloses prospective tariff/trade-investigation risk, but the supplied filing does not quantify exposure or establish a new tariff outcome.

claims.text: A January 15, 2026 BIS final rule moved qualifying H200/equivalent and less-advanced semiconductor exports to China/Macau from presumptive denial to case-by-case review, subject to technical thresholds and certifications. NVIDIA nevertheless disclosed that, as of the end of FY2027 Q2, it was effectively foreclosed from China’s data-center compute market and could not deliver a competitively viable product approved by both governments; it also disclosed a 25% tariff on H200s shipped under the licensing program and said it had not passed that tariff to customers.

For NVDA, a further tightening, license denial/delay, or Chinese product-use restriction can impair addressable data-center demand and reinforce competitor ecosystems; a license relaxation is only optional upside, not a restoration assumption, because Chinese approval and product competitiveness remain separate constraints. Taiwan and South Korea supply continuity is a second geographic transmission channel disclosed by NVIDIA.

Downside policy scenario: a renewed broader export restriction, adverse license decision/condition, or new constraint on Taiwan/South Korea supply would preserve or deepen China-data-center exclusion and/or disrupt components, weakening the business assumption embedded in demand-led valuation cases. View-change discriminator: an authoritative rule/license action plus NVIDIA disclosure that it can—or cannot—ship a competitive China data-center system with approvals from both governments.

Micron’s June 2026 10-Q says the April 2025 Section 232 semiconductor investigation and February 2026 announced Section 301 investigations had uncertain scope/outcomes and could lead to industry-wide tariffs or trade restrictions. It identifies transmission through higher product/material/equipment costs, customer demand effects, supply-chain changes, and mitigation costs or manufacturing delays.

MU’s supplied disclosure supports a conditional trade-cost and customer-demand risk rather than a measured current loss: a final tariff or restriction could raise input/selling costs and interfere with customer products containing Micron solutions, while no supplied source quantifies Micron’s affected revenue, manufacturing geography, or pass-through.

Downside policy scenario: a final Section 232 or Section 301 measure that covers Micron-relevant semiconductors, manufacturing equipment, materials, or derivative products could raise costs, delay mitigation and weaken demand. View-change discriminator: final government scope/rates/exclusions together with Micron’s subsequent disclosure of affected sourcing, customer demand, or mitigation costs; relaxation/no covered final action would remove this particular incremental risk channel.

gaps.description: The January 2026 BIS rule is dated primary text, but no post-January complete legal-status review is supplied; it cannot establish all current amendments, license outcomes, or applicability to each issuer beyond NVIDIA’s own later disclosure.

Neither supplied policy disclosure provides revenue by end-demand country, customer domicile, manufacturing location, affected product, or a tariff/pass-through/loss coefficient. Therefore policy financial impact and a policy-based NVDA-versus-MU preference are not quantified.

assumptions: Policy scenarios are conditional and do not assume a future license approval, rule change, tariff imposition, Chinese approval, or supply disruption.
Billing/customer location, end demand, and manufacturing location are treated as distinct; no revenue or supply weight is inferred from the disclosures.
The January BIS rule is used as dated legal text only; current completeness is unverified.
arguments.counter_thesis: NVDA’s January rule created a case-by-case pathway for qualifying products, so a supported license plus both-government product acceptance could restore some optional China access. Conversely, MU’s cited investigations may end without measures material to Micron. Neither result is established by the supplied record.

review_conditions.description: Review NVDA’s policy case if BIS issues a new/revised advanced-computing rule or a material license decision, or if NVIDIA states that a competitive China data-center system has gained (or failed to gain) both U.S. and Chinese approval; this would change the China-access assumption.

Review MU’s policy case when Section 232 or Section 301 reaches a final scope/rate/exemption decision or Micron quantifies sourcing, costs, delays, or customer-demand effects; this would convert a conditional channel into an assessable impact.

shared_exposures.mechanism: Both companies face U.S. trade-policy transmission into semiconductor demand and supply chains, but the disclosed channels differ: NVDA reports active China data-center access constraints and overseas-partner dependency, while MU reports uncertain potential tariff/trade-investigation effects. No shared financial weight or common loss percentage is established.
shared_exposures.qualification: This is a qualitative common exposure only; it does not establish equivalent legal applicability, revenue exposure, manufacturing exposure, or policy sensitivity.

agent_report.work_summary: Reviewed the supplied BIS final-rule excerpt and the latest supplied NVIDIA and Micron SEC policy/geography excerpts. Focused on legal status, issuer-described operating channels, and discriminators rather than valuation or price behavior.
main_conclusions: NVDA’s filing identifies an already-operational China data-center access constraint despite a case-by-case licensing pathway.
NVDA’s disclosed Taiwan/South Korea supply reliance adds a distinct geographic disruption channel.
MU discloses possible tariff/trade-restriction channels, but supplied evidence does not establish a final measure or quantify exposure.
Policy evidence does not support a quantified relative preference between NVDA and MU.
agent_report.short_summary: NVDA has the clearer, currently disclosed policy constraint: China data-center compute access remains effectively foreclosed in its filing. MU’s trade exposure is presently a conditional investigation/tariff risk rather than a measured impact.
limitations: No complete post-January 2026 legal-status review or verified license decisions were supplied.
No issuer revenue, customer end-demand, manufacturing, sourcing, or pass-through weights were available for the policy channels.
This role did not assess valuation, consensus, or market technicals.
